title: Drain the queue
briefing: ~/queue holds pending jobs (job1.txt, job2.txt, job3.txt). Process them:
move every job into ~/processed until the queue is empty.
You don't know how many there'll be next time — so loop until the queue
runs dry. That's what `while` does: repeat as long as a condition holds.
tips: `while [ -n "$(ls ~/queue)" ]; do ...; done` repeats while `ls ~/queue` still prints something.
objective: Move every file out of ~/queue into ~/processed, leaving ~/queue empty.
expert_objective: Empty ~/queue by moving each job into ~/processed.
hints: Loop while the queue isn't empty: `while [ -n "$(ls ~/queue)" ]; do ...; done`. `$(...)` runs a command and drops its output in place; `[ -n ... ]` is true when that text isn't empty.
Inside, move one job: `f=$(ls ~/queue | head -1); mv ~/queue/$f ~/processed/`. (A `for f in ~/queue/*; do mv "$f" ~/processed/; done` works too.)
solution:
mkdir ~/processed
for f in ~/queue/*; do mv "$f" ~/processed/; done
explanation: A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition keeps succeeding — perfect when you don't know the count in advance (drain a queue, retry until something's ready). Here the condition uses `$(...)`, which runs a command and substitutes its output, and `[ -n ... ]` to ask 'is there still anything there?'.
